title: Foreword
text: The Foreword, written by the Ahl al-Bayt World Assembly (ABWA), frames the book as part of a broader project defending the sanctity of the Islamic message. It states that the arguments of scholars belonging to the School of the Ahl al-Bayt are based on genuine scholarship and appeal to reason, avoiding prejudice and bias. The Assembly expresses gratitude to the author, Professor Murtada Mutahhari, and the translator, Mrs. Zaynab Muhammadi 'Iraqi.

title: Introduction — The problem of dissimilar Imam methodologies
text: Mutahhari opens by posing the central problem of the book: Imam al-Husayn's approach (open revolt against Yazid) appears to contradict the approach of the other Imams, including 'Ali, al-Hassan, al-Sajjad and al-Sadiq, all of whom practiced taqiyyah (dissimulation) at various points. If dissimulation was religiously justified, why did al-Husayn not use it despite having the grounds to do so? If it was not justified, why did the other Imams use it and command their followers to do so? This is a fundamental debate regardless of whether the Imams' methodologies were similar or different.

title: Introduction — Taqiyyah and the richness/danger of having many Imams
text: Taqiyyah (dissimulation, hiding one's beliefs under pressure) is closely associated with Shi'ism. Because the Shi'ah accept the sayings and deeds of fourteen infallibles as testament (more numerous even than the hadiths in the Sunni Sihah al-Sittah — Al-Kafi alone reportedly contains more than 16,000 hadiths), Shi'ism has never needed qiyas (analogical reasoning) or istihsan (juristic preference). But this richness is also a danger: fourteen leaders announcing different routes and traditions, without careful research, can be exploited by those who wish to use religion for their own immoral aims, producing chaos, dispersal and a lack of morals — 'once a patient has too many doctors, there is no hope for recovery.'

title: Introduction — Imam al-Sadiq and the wealthy man's house
text: Apparent contradictions between the Imams' lifestyles (the Prophet and 'Ali living in poverty and patched clothing vs. Imam al-Hassan, al-Sadiq and al-Rida living well) are resolved by recognizing that religion adapts its expression to the exigencies of time, while its essence (sympathy, compassion, equality, justice, fairness) stays constant. Imam al-Sadiq once visited a wealthy man living in a small house who explained he kept his late father's house; the Imam replied: 'If your father was lacking common sense, does that mean you should be foolish like he was?' — establishing that inherited custom is not itself a religious value.

title: Introduction — Sufyan al-Thawri's objection to Imam al-Sadiq's fine clothing
text: Sufyan al-Thawri objected to Imam al-Sadiq wearing fine clothing, since the Prophet did not. The Imam replied that the Prophet lived a middle-class lifestyle appropriate to his own time and that Islam does not command any particular manner of dress; it commands sympathy, compassion, equality, justice and fairness. 'As you see me now, I am aware of the responsibilities towards my possessions, thus there is no logical or spiritual difference between my method and the Prophet's.' During a famine in Imam al-Sadiq's time, he ordered his stocked wheat sold in the market and bought ordinary market bread (mixed oat and wheat) for his own household, illustrating fairness over ritualized asceticism.

title: Introduction — 'Ali and the tradition on dyeing the beard
text: A second example: 'Ali used to narrate the hadith 'Color the white hairs in the beard and do not let yourselves resemble the Jews' but never acted upon it himself. He explained that the order was a wartime tactic specific to the Prophet's time (so the enemy could not distinguish old soldiers from young in the army), not a permanent religious commandment. Mutahhari uses this and the Imam al-Sadiq clothing example to introduce the interpretive method of 'conventional reconciliation' (al-jam' al-'urfi) — resolving apparent contradictions between the Imams' practices by attending to the necessities of their respective times, rather than assuming a fixed literal command binding for all eras.

title: Ch1 — 'Ali's reluctance to accept the caliphate
text: 'Ali initially refused the caliphate after 'Uthman's assassination despite people insisting on swearing allegiance to him, saying (Nahj al-Balaghah, Sermon 91): 'Leave me and seek someone else. We are facing a matter that has several sides and colors, which neither hearts can bear nor intelligence fathom... You should know that if I respond to you, I will lead you as I know how (not how you want me to)... At present, I would rather stay a minister than to become a chief.' Mutahhari reads this as 'Ali foreseeing the immense problems that would in fact later materialize during his caliphate.

title: Ch1 — 'Uthman's assassination and the problem of hypocrisy
text: 'Ali inherited a caliphate poisoned by 'Uthman's assassination. 'Ali had acted as mediator between 'Uthman and the revolutionaries, disagreeing with 'Uthman's favoritism toward relatives but also opposing 'opening the door' to killing a caliph. Mu'awiyah covertly worked to escalate the unrest that led to 'Uthman's murder, then exploited it for his own political advantage — sending 'Uthman's blood-stained shirt and his wife's severed fingers to Damascus, hanging them up, and inciting the people to avenge 'Uthman's blood against 'Ali. Unlike the Prophet's opponents (open polytheists under the slogan 'Long Live Hubal'), 'Ali faced an intelligent, non-religious group that pretended to follow Islam while pursuing anti-Islamic aims — using Qur'an 17:33 ('whosoever is killed unjustly, we have given his heir authority') as a deceptive slogan despite Mu'awiyah having no real kinship claim to 'Uthman's blood. This led directly to the battles of Jamal and Siffin.

title: Ch1 — Inflexibility in justice and bluntness in politics
text: 'Ali refused to allocate special subsidies to influential people (a custom that had crept in after the Prophet's death), saying: 'Are you asking me to gain victory and success in politics at the price of oppression and destroying the rights of powerless people?! I swear upon the Almighty, as long as there is day and night in this world, I will not do such a thing.' His bluntness and honesty in politics also drew criticism from his own supporters, who argued 'some dishonesty and deception is necessary' in politics and unfavorably compared him to the more 'tactful' Mu'awiyah. 'Ali responded (Sermon 199) that Mu'awiyah is not more cunning than him — 'he is deceitful... If Allah did not consider deception as his enemy, you would have seen that 'Ali would have been the most cunning of all people' — but that such deceitfulness is immoral, evil, wicked and blasphemous.

title: Ch1 — Why the Kharijites were 'Ali's fundamental problem: the Prophet's 13-year training period vs. 'Ali's untrained converts
text: Mutahhari explains the structural cause of the Kharijite problem. During his 13 years in Mecca, the Prophet trained a small, deeply grounded core group before any war was permitted — even under torture, he refused permission for jihad, consenting only to emigration. This created a group (~1,000 by the time of migration) who deeply understood Islam's essence, not just its outward form. Under the later caliphs, especially 'Uthman's, this training method was neglected in favor of rapid conquest, producing a new class of Muslims familiar only with Islam's outward 'crust' — exemplified by people with calloused foreheads from excessive prostration, described by Ibn 'Abbas after visiting the future rebels: 'Their foreheads are wounded because of excessive prostrations; they have hands that have calluses like the knee of a camel... Most manifest are their resolute and indomitable faces.' 'Ali described this class bluntly: 'They are a people who are rough, remorseless, tough, hard-hearted, rude, but with inferior, slavish characters and spirits... They do not know what the Qur'an is. They do not understand the meaning of the Qur'an.'

title: Ch1 — The Qur'ans-on-spears stratagem at Siffin
text: At Siffin, when Mu'awiyah and 'Amr ibn al-'As realized they were losing, they ordered Qur'ans raised on spear-points, provoking the untrained pietist faction within 'Ali's own army to refuse to keep fighting ('We shall not fight the Qur'an'). 'Ali objected: 'They have not brought forward the Qur'an itself but its papers and cover so that they can rise up again against this very Qur'an... I am your imam. I am your speaking Qur'an.' The faction accused 'Ali of having his own ambitions and refused to continue. When Malik al-Ashtar was on the verge of victory, they threatened to kill 'Ali himself unless Malik was recalled (they numbered about 20,000); 'Ali sent word for Malik to return.

title: Ch1 — Arbitration, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and the birth of Kharijite doctrine
text: The faction insisted on arbitration and rejected 'Ali's proposed arbitrators (Ibn 'Abbas, then Malik al-Ashtar), instead forcing Abu Musa al-Ash'ari on him — a former governor 'Ali had removed, and 'in his heart an enemy of 'Ali.' Abu Musa was outmaneuvered by 'Amr ibn al-'As in the arbitration. Realizing they had been tricked, the faction did not conclude that they erred in halting the fight or in choosing Abu Musa; instead they declared that appointing any human arbitrator was itself blasphemy, citing Qur'an 6:57 ('The judgment belongs to none but Allah'), and demanded 'Ali repent alongside them for having become 'a non-believer like us.' 'Ali refused: 'Arbitration is no blasphemy. You do not understand the meaning of the verse... I shall never confess to a sin I have never committed.' They split from him, forming the Kharijite sect ('the rebels against 'Ali').

title: Ch1 — 'Ali's tolerance of the Kharijites before their armed revolt
text: 'Ali tolerated the Kharijites' open disrespect for a long period before they turned to armed insurrection: he never cut their share of the treasury or restricted their freedom. When a Kharijite in the crowd cursed him after a masterful answer to a question ('May Allah kill him, how knowledgeable he is'), 'Ali stopped his companions from retaliating: 'Leave him be. He cursed me. The most you can do to him is to curse him. Leave him alone.' During prayer, a Kharijite named Ibn al-Kawwab repeatedly interrupted 'Ali by reciting Qur'an 39:65 (implying his deeds were nullified by 'polytheism'); 'Ali, obeying 7:204 ('when the Qur'an is recited, listen and keep silent'), stayed silent each time, then on the third or fourth repetition recited 30:60 ('let not those who have no certitude make you unstable') and continued his prayer without further reaction.

title: Ch1 — The Kharijite sect's formal doctrines
text: The Kharijites formalized their break into a religious sect with explicit doctrines: (1) 'Uthman, 'Ali, Mu'awiyah, and all who accepted arbitration are non-believers, except those who repented; (2) 'enjoining good and forbidding evil' is obligatory and unconditional — one must rise against any unlawful or cruel ruler even believing the rising will fail; (3) faith is inseparable from action — a single major sin (lying, drinking, backbiting) expels a person from Islam entirely. The practical result: they considered themselves the only true Muslims, declared others' meat forbidden and intermarriage forbidden, and — most extremely — considered killing the women and children of non-Kharijites permissible. They killed a passing companion of the Prophet and his pregnant wife (ripping open her stomach) for refusing to disown 'Ali, and rebuked a man for eating a single date from an unattended garden as 'intruding on your Muslim brother's wealth.'

title: Ch1 — Nahrawan: negotiation, the banner, and the battle
text: When the Kharijites' actions escalated from words to violence, 'Ali confronted them at Nahrawan. Ibn 'Abbas was sent first but achieved nothing. 'Ali then spoke to them himself; of roughly 12,000, 8,000 repented under the protective banner 'Ali raised, and 4,000 refused and were killed in battle, with only about 10 survivors — including 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, 'Ali's future assassin. 'Ali's own verdict on the act (Sermon 92): 'It was I and I alone who removed the eye of this revolt. No one save me could have stopped them with his sword.' He explained that no ordinary believer would have had the nerve to draw a sword against people who appeared more pious and ascetic than himself — 'their hands would shiver, their heart would tremble' — and that only an unbeliever, acting for the wrong reasons, could otherwise have done it. He used the image of kalab (rabies): the Kharijites were like rabid dogs whose disease (fanatical false piety) would spread to whoever they bit, so that eradication, though tragic, was necessary to save the wider body of Islam from 'rigidity, petrifaction, idiocy and ignorance.'

title: Ch1 — Characteristics of the Kharijites: bravery, worship, ignorance
text: Mutahhari lists their distinguishing traits: extraordinary bravery and devotion to their cause; excessive, dogmatic worship (the source of their apparent piety and the reason no ordinary Muslim dared oppose them); and above all ignorance and lack of real Islamic knowledge, which 'Ali called their defining vice: 'You are the worst of people... because you are spears in the hands of the devil. Satan places you in his bow instead of his arrows and crushes his targets with you.' Mutahhari notes that Mu'awiyah and 'Amr ibn al-'As — genuine hypocrites who privately respected 'Ali (Mu'awiyah reportedly wept when 'Ali was later described to him, saying 'Time can never again bring a person like 'Ali') — deliberately used ignorant pietist factions as tools to achieve their political ends, a pattern Mutahhari says recurs 'in various guises' throughout history.

title: Ch1 — The Iqbal/Ja'far-Sadiq rumor as a modern parable of Kharijite-style ignorance
text: Mutahhari recounts a contemporary anecdote: a rumor spread that the poet Muhammad Iqbal had cursed Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq in his writing, based on a couplet actually condemning two historical traitors coincidentally also named Ja'far (of Bengal) and Sadiq (of Deccan) who betrayed Muslim rulers to British colonizers. Mutahhari traces the rumor to its source and shows it to be a complete misreading, using it as a direct parallel to Kharijite-style thinking: declaring people non-believers or heretics based on surface impressions without careful investigation. He urges: 'Investigate! Investigate... then say whatever you want, but do not say anything before you have done your research,' explicitly invoking the Nahrawan Kharijites as the cautionary example ('Do not be like the Nahrawan Kharijites').

title: Ch1 — Ibn Muljam, Qatam, and the assassination plot
text: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam was one of nine ascetic Kharijites who vowed in Mecca that 'Ali, Mu'awiyah and 'Amr ibn al-'As were the causes of all the Muslim world's strife, and drew lots to assassinate each; Ibn Muljam was assigned 'Ali. In Kufah he fell in love with a Kharijite woman, Qatam, whose father and brother 'Ali had killed at Nahrawan. She agreed to marry him only on the condition — as her fourth and final dowry demand, after money, a slave boy, and a slave girl — that he kill 'Ali: 'If you seek union with me, you must kill 'Ali. If you live, you will gain what you seek, and if you die, then nothing.' He composed verses declaring no dowry in the world was as exalted as 'Ali's blood. The date chosen was the night before the 19th of Ramadan, deliberately selected — per Ibn Abi al-Hadid — because the Kharijites believed killing 'Ali on the Night of Qadr (Laylat al-Qadr) would earn greater heavenly reward.

title: Ch1 — 'Ali's final instruction on the Kharijites and his death
text: On his deathbed, 'Ali distinguished the danger of Mu'awiyah's hypocrites from that of the Kharijites and instructed his followers: 'After me, do not kill the Kharijites anymore, because whoever seeks truth and commits a mistake is not the same as the one who seeks falsehood from the beginning and has reached it' — since killing them further would only serve Mu'awiyah's interests, not truth and justice. When Ibn Muljam was captured and brought before the dying 'Ali, 'Ali asked him, 'Why did you do such a thing? Was I a bad Imam for you?' Ibn Muljam, unrepentant, said he had vowed to kill the worst of God's creatures with that sword; 'Ali replied that his prayer had indeed been answered, since he himself would be killed by that same sword. 'Ali died on the night of the 21st of Ramadan and was buried in secret by his closest family, his grave's location concealed for about a hundred years — out of fear the Kharijites would desecrate it — until Imam al-Sadiq revealed it publicly after the Umayyad dynasty's fall.
